samples: This program prints a plain-text statement for two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one row per customer in alphabetical order showing the name, the number of lines and the discounted total in fixed-width columns, followed by a grand total of all invoices. It reuses an `invoice` module that computes each total as the sum of quantity times unit price, minus a percentage discount, rounded to cents. It needs only console access and reads no input, so it works as a demo or formatting template, but you would need to replace the sample data to use it on real invoices.

This program prints a fixed-column plain-text statement for two built-in sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one row per customer sorted by name, showing the number of lines and the total after any percentage discount, followed by a grand total across all invoices. It reuses the `invoice` module for the totals, which are exact decimals rounded to cents. It only writes to the console and takes no input, so it works as a demo or formatting template, and you would need to replace the hard-coded sample data to report on real invoices.

This program prints a plain-text statement for two built-in sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one fixed-column row per customer in alphabetical order showing the number of lines and the discounted total, followed by a grand total of all invoices. It reuses the `invoice` module to compute each total (line quantity times price, less a percentage discount, rounded to cents), and it only needs console access, so it reads no files and uses no network. It is a demo rather than a general tool: the invoices are hard-coded in `main`, so you would need to supply your own data or call `statement_line` and `grand_total` from other code to use it for real work.

This program prints a fixed-column text statement for two hard-coded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), one row per customer sorted by name showing the customer, number of lines and discounted total, followed by a grand total of all invoice totals. It reuses an `invoice` module that computes each invoice's total by summing quantity times unit price and then applying a percentage discount, rounded to cents. It only needs console output and does not read real data, so it works as a demo or template, and you would need to replace the sample invoices to use it for anything real.

This program prints a plain-text statement for two hardcoded sample invoices (ACME and Globex), with one fixed-column row per customer showing the number of lines and the discounted total, sorted by customer name, followed by a grand total of all invoices. Totals come from the separate `invoice` module, which applies a percentage discount and rounds to cents. It only needs console access and takes no input, so it is a demo or template rather than a tool for real data, unless you swap in your own invoices.
